Why did Facebook become so popular? Is that just because of concentration effect?
Prior to FB everyone used myspace and at the time FB was the perfect alternative to bug-riddled myspace. Now they monopolized the whole internet so there is no alternative.

Facebook made some very smart decisions early on. That, combined with arriving on the webs at a near-perfect time, helped it become so successful. MySpace was bloated, and its new owners, News Corp, cared more about gutting it for profit than building a lasting social network. It was full of spam profiles and fake names.

Facebook, on the other hand, was minimalistic and streamlined. It didn't require various clicks to leave a comment on someone's page. There was more conversation. It was also "cool," because college students were the first ones using it. Zuckerberg didn't sell. He took venture capital instead of polluting the site with ads. He also met with successful businessmen when considering the site's future.

Side note: Tom Anderson once wanted to charge for the basic MySpace service, Chris DeWolfe suggested keeping it free. So from the beginning, MySpace and Facebook had opposite corporate values.

I see the original Facebook settlers as people who were just "passing through" MySpace, which was never much of a home. Nomads, I suppose.

Google+ committed seppuku. It was a helluva lot more modern than Facebook, but no one wants to use a social network unless their friends are also using it. That's kinda the point. Google+ was invite-only for an unnecessarily long time, and unlike Facebook, which grew with demand, Google shut out demand until people were like "fuck it, I didn't really care that much anyway."

Facebook, on the other hand, was minimalistic and streamlined. It didn't require various clicks to leave a comment on someone's page

This is probably the biggest factor if you ask me. It doesn't require anything other than just mindlessly scrolling down endlessly and occasionally clicking like, occasionally responding to a message, occasionally commenting on a post. It's such a low effort instant gratification process that it clicked instantly with the mindless droves of the general population. Literally everything on there is low effort and a disgusting amount of people's news and information derives from memes, yes, memes, entirely taken at face value because people are too lazy and stupid to look anything up themselves let alone have an informed opinion on it. That's why all these emojis got streamlined next to 'likes' that convey various emotions, it's another simple low effort method for people to communicate without having to actually engage with other people. Apathy sells way better than sex.
Google + was years later ... FB was already entering grandparents market.
Cauae they didn't sell out. Every company to try to benefit from an established social environment has failed.

FB was about 5-6 when they announced they were doing an API. My space was already shit and HiFive was rolling along really well.

But that API turned into games and shit. So people stuck around and kuckberg didn't sell out. People probably liked that attitude.

If another site had competed at an APi level things might have been different.

At the beginning, they deliberately made it students only and invite-only. People felt they were in an exclusive club. It was special to be invited and in, and it was full of people they had reasons to communicate with - fellow students, 'interesting' young minds, and so on. People felt comfortable sharing private stuff because it was more like a virtual Spring Break with like-minded young people and not all the strange people like MySpace.

The simple user interface and the refusal to put much advertisement in added to the 'good vibes'.

There was also no hint at the time how much the user profiles were exploited for targeted advertisement and such - or to de-anonymise visits to 'unrelated' sites.

MySpace management didn't get at all how much value they could get from just collecting data of their users - trying to make money in other ways instead. Advertisement market was also much smaller at the time, as the big money had not yet warmed up to digital marketing. And they let everyone do whatever they want, leading to bizarre, flashy and annoying personal pages which were not easy to go through. The news were underdeveloped, you had to delve into those bizarre home pages. Eventually, it also lost the 'in' factor, and then everyone left.

Facebook also had a few times were such issues threatened them - but were quicker to adapt. The second generation didn't want to be seen doing everything by their parents, so privacy was improved. And so on.

Other competitors didn't have any vision - Germany had a student site which did the same and was very successful. But it had it's market in the name, and when Facebook opened up, they weren't able to follow, became irrelevant, and died.

I also like the subtle but effective ways of Facebook to protect people who have more exposure (work in a big company or such) from crazies from all over the world. I don't think any other social network is remotely close to that.

Facebook also offers quite a bit - you get lots of information about friends, family, colleagues, and so on. And only give comparably little information about yourself.

I personally always assume that someone is 'shady' or wears a lot of aluminum on their head if they don't at least have a minor presence there. And I'm pretty sure I'm not the only one who thinks like that.
